previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, COPD, and chronic kidney disease was admitted for recurrent syncope associated with coughing. He presented with worsening orthopnea, PND, and fluid overload, consistent with acute on chronic systolic heart failure. His syncope episodes were directly linked to coughing fits, with no evidence of arrhythmia or seizure activity. He was treated with IV furosemide, achieving a discharge weight of 82.4 kg, close to his dry weight. His cough improved with optimized GERD treatment (increased omeprazole and added ranitidine), azithromycin for COPD, and increased evening gabapentin. He remained free of syncope during admission. A right upper lobe nodule was noted, with follow-up recommended. He was discharged home with medication adjustments and plans for outpatient follow-up in cardiology, pulmonology, and primary care.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old male with PMH significant for 
systolic CHF (nonischemic cardiomyopathy with EF of ___ 
___, CKD, COPD (on 2L NC at home), IDDM with multiple 
recent admissions for heart failure exacerbation who is now 
presenting with substantial weight gain (89.8kg from dry weight 
of 82kg) as well as multiple syncopal episodes.  

ACUTE ISSUES
============

# Acute on chronic systolic CHF: Hemodynamically stable, 
evidenced by worsening of orthopnea, PND, and significant JVP 
elevation on exam. BNP within recent baseline but clinically he 
appeared overloaded at admission. LVEF ___ on most recent 
___ TTE, ___ III-IV. He was treated with 100mg IV lasix 
bolus, lasix drip up to 20mg/hr, and 2.5 metolazone on ___. He 
decreased to his dry weight, 82.2kg. He remains on pravastatin, 
losartan, digoxin, and aspirin. He could not be started on a 
beta-blocker due to ongoing cocaine use. At discharge, he was 
stabilized on 100mg torsemide BID and 2.5mg metolazone weekly on 
___. He will need repeat labs on ___ (script 
written) and he will follow-up with his cardiologist, Dr. ___.

# Syncope: His syncope has been recurrent and associated with 
deep coughing episodes. Given the direct association with these 
episodes and his known cardiopulmonary disease, there is concern 
that he has transiently reduced cerebral perfusion due to 
decreased preload when he increases his intrathoracic pressure. 
No clinical evidence of seizures outside of some urinary 
incontinence when he syncopizes, though he immediately regains 
consciousness without post-ictal state. Per ENT evaluation, 
there was no vocal cord dysfunction on nasopharyngoscopy. Per 
pulmonary consult, we optimized medications for his GERD 
(increased PPI dose and added ranitidine), COPD (started 
azithromycin course), as well as symptomatic treatment with 
benzonatate and increased dose of gabapentin. His telemetry did 
not show any significant arrhythmias, and he did not have any 
episodes of syncope or presyncope during this admission. 
Orthostatics were negative: 95/54 and 104 recumbent, 90/60 and 
104 sitting, 94/61 and 104 standing. It is possible his recent 
cocaine use caused a tachyarrhythmia that led to his syncopal 
episodes. He had no signs of infection. The patient reported 
significantly improved cough by the day of discharge and had no 
syncopal or pre-syncopal episodes during this admission.
 
CHRONIC ISSUES
==============

# COPD: PFTs ___ with FEV1 68%, FEV1/FVC 97%. At baseline, 
patient on 2L home O2. However, with diuresis in-house, he 
improved to 92-99% on room air. He was  continues on duonebs and 
benzonatate, with significant improvement in his cough. He was 
discharged on home albuterol and benzonatate.

# T2DM: Due to significant requirements on ISS in-house, his 
glargine was increased to 40u at bedtime. He was also continued 
on humalog sliding scale and a diabetic diet.

# Cocaine-induced cardiomyopathy ___ substance abuse: It was 
noted that he would not be an ICD candidate due to ongoing drug 
use. He was educated on the importance of abstaining from 
cocaine and any other illicit drug use. 

# Tobacco use: He was continued on his home nicotine patch 14mg 
daily.  
# HLD: He was continued on home pravastatin in-house and at 
discharge.
# HTN: He was continued on home losartan in-house and at 
discharge.  
# Gout: He was continued on home colchicine in-house and at 
discharge.
# Anxiety/Insomnia: He was continued on home diphenhydramine, 
lorazepam, and trazodone prn in-house and at discharge.
# GERD: He was continued on home omeprazole and ranitidine 
in-house and at discharge.
# Chronic pain: He was continued on home tramadol and gabapentin 
(renally-dosed) in-house and at discharge.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure caring for you during your stay at ___. You 
were recently admitted to ___ for weight gain caused by heart 
failure, as well as several episodes of fainting.  You were 
given lasix IV and metolazone, which resulted in a significant 
loss of the excess fluid such that you returned to your usual 
weight of ~ 180lbs. Your lightheadedness episodes were primarily 
triggered by coughing spells, which decreased while you were in 
the hospital. You did not have further episodes of fainting and 
your heart monitor did not show any abnormal rhythms. We also 
found that there was cocaine in your system from your urine 
test.  We strongly encourage you to stop using all 
recreational/illicit drugs because these can cause serious 
damage to your heart and may very well be causing you to black 
out. You were stabilized on torsemide 100mg twice daily as well 
as metolazone 2.5mg weekly on ___. You were also started 
on potassium supplementation. Please be sure to attend your 
appointment at the ___ clinic on ___, where you 
will have labs checked. Please weigh yourself every morning, 
call your doctor if weight goes up more than 3 lbs in 2 days or 
more than 5 lbs in 5 days. Please keep all your appointments 
with your heart failure team after you are discharged to prevent 
extra fluid from building up again.  

We wish you all the best!

Your ___ care team
